decision.explanation: Let F(x,y,z)=ln(2x+y)-z. Its gradient at (1,-1,0) is (2,1,-1), a normal vector. Thus the normal line is (x-1)/2=y+1=-z, which is option e.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem: Find the equation of the normal line to the surface $z=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)$ at the point $(1,-1,0).$
after.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y) \\ 0 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)-z\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, if we set $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)-z$, then our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(1,-1,0)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,-1,0).$

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(1,-1,0):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)-z)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)-z)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)-z)k \\  & =\frac{2}{2x+y}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{2x+y}\text{ }j-1\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,-1,0) & =\frac{2}{2(1)+(-1)}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{2(1)+(-1)}\text{ }j-k \\  & =2\text{ }i+\,j-k \\  & =⟨2,\,1,\,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by using the symmetric form of the equation of the line that is parallel to the vector $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$,  we get: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y-(-1)}{1}=\frac{z-0}{-1} \\ \frac{x-1}{2}=y+1=-z\end{aligned}
$$

content.problem: Find the equation of the normal line to the surface $z=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)$ at the point $(1,-1,0).$
content.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y) \\ 0 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)-z\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, if we set $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)-z$, then our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(1,-1,0)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,-1,0).$

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(1,-1,0):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)-z)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)-z)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)-z)k \\  & =\frac{2}{2x+y}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{2x+y}\text{ }j-1\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,-1,0) & =\frac{2}{2(1)+(-1)}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{2(1)+(-1)}\text{ }j-k \\  & =2\text{ }i+\,j-k \\  & =⟨2,\,1,\,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by using the symmetric form of the equation of the line that is parallel to the vector $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$,  we get: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y-(-1)}{1}=\frac{z-0}{-1} \\ \frac{x-1}{2}=y+1=-z\end{aligned}
$$

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,1)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(1,-1,1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$  and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}-2yz+z)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2}-2yz+z)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(x{y}^{2}-2yz+z)\,k \\  & ={y}^{2}\text{ }i+(2xy-2z)\text{ }j+(-2y+1)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,-1,1) & =(-1)^{2}\,i+(2(1)(-1)-2(1))\,j+(-2(-1)+1)\,k \\  & =1\,i-4j+3\,k\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, $\,i-4\,j+3\,k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,1).$

after.problem: Consider the plane curve $\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}=1.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(0,4).$
after.worked_solution:
If we set $f(x,y)=\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=1.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(0,4)$ can be found by computing $∇f(0,4).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(0,4):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{9})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{9})\,j \\  & =-\frac{2}{9}x\,i+\frac{1}{8}y\,j \\ ∇f(0,4) & =-\frac{2}{9}(0)\,i+\frac{1}{8}(4)\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\,j \\  & =⟨0,\frac{1}{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(0,4)=⟨0,\frac{1}{2}⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(0,4).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-{x}_{0}){v}_{y}-(y-{y}_{0}){v}_{x} & =0 \\ (x-0)\frac{1}{2}-(y-4)0 & =0 \\ \frac{1}{2}x & =0 \\ x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to v=⟨vx,vy⟩ and passes through the point (x0,y0) can be written as:

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of the Normal Line to a Plane Curve Using the Gradient
content.problem: Consider the plane curve $\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}=1.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(0,4).$
content.worked_solution:
If we set $f(x,y)=\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=1.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(0,4)$ can be found by computing $∇f(0,4).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(0,4):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{9})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{9})\,j \\  & =-\frac{2}{9}x\,i+\frac{1}{8}y\,j \\ ∇f(0,4) & =-\frac{2}{9}(0)\,i+\frac{1}{8}(4)\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\,j \\  & =⟨0,\frac{1}{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(0,4)=⟨0,\frac{1}{2}⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(0,4).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-{x}_{0}){v}_{y}-(y-{y}_{0}){v}_{x} & =0 \\ (x-0)\frac{1}{2}-(y-4)0 & =0 \\ \frac{1}{2}x & =0 \\ x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
If we set $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=3.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(-1,-1,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(-1,-1,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(-1,-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})k \\  & =2x\text{ }i+2y\text{ }j+2z\text{ }k \\ ∇f(-1,-1,1) & =2(-1)\text{ }i+2(-1)\text{ }j+2(1)\text{ }k \\  & =-2\,i-2\,j+2\,k \\  & =⟨-2,-2,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=3.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(-1,-1,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(-1,-1,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(-1,-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})k \\  & =2x\text{ }i+2y\text{ }j+2z\text{ }k \\ ∇f(-1,-1,1) & =2(-1)\text{ }i+2(-1)\text{ }j+2(1)\text{ }k \\  & =-2\,i-2\,j+2\,k \\  & =⟨-2,-2,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-(-1)}{-2}=\frac{y-(-1)}{-2}=\frac{z-1}{2} \\ \frac{x+1}{-2}=\frac{y+1}{-2}=\frac{z-1}{2} \\ \frac{x+1}{1}=\frac{y+1}{1}=\frac{z-1}{-1} \\ x+1=y+1=\frac{z-1}{-1}\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=x{e}^{y}+y{e}^{z}+z{e}^{x},$ find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(0,0,1).$
after.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(0,0,1)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(0,0,1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(0,0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{e}^{y}+y{e}^{z}+z{e}^{x})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{e}^{y}+y{e}^{z}+z{e}^{x})\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(x{e}^{y}+y{e}^{z}+z{e}^{x})\,k \\  & =({e}^{y}+z{e}^{x})\,i+(x{e}^{y}+{e}^{z})\,j+(y{e}^{z}+{e}^{x})\,k \\ ∇f(0,0,1) & =({e}^{0}+(1){e}^{0})i+((0){e}^{0}+{e}^{1})j+((0){e}^{1}+{e}^{0})k \\  & =2\,i+e\,j+k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $2\,i+e\,j+k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(0,0,1).$

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at (x,y,z)=(0,0,1):

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z) j+fz(x,y,z) k=∂∂x(xey+yez+zex)i+∂∂y(xey+yez+zex)j+∂∂z(xey+yez+zex)k=(ey+zex)i+(xey+ez)j+(yez+ex)k∇f(0,0,1)=(e0+(1)e0)i+((0)e0+e1)j+((0)e1+e0)k=2i+ej+k

Therefore, 2i+ej+k is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(0,0,1).
